Part 1 of 7

A New Consumer Culture

CORE OBJECTIVE

Core Objective 1: Assess the impact of the consumer culture that emerged in America during the 1920s and explain the factors that contributed to its growth.

IN MY WORDS: What is a consumer culture? Name one thing that helped it grow in the 1920s.

Reading ABoom Times and a “Consumer Culture”

During the 1920s, the U.S. economy became the envy of the world. Following the brief recession in 1920–1921, Americans benefited from the fastest economic growth in history. Between 1922 and 1928, industrial production soared by 70 percent. Jobs were plentiful, inflation was low, and average personal income rose steadily.

Perhaps the most visible change during the 1920s was the emergence of a powerful “consumer culture” in which mass production and consumption of nationally advertised products dictated much of social life and social status. For many Americans (most notably the business interests that profited from it), the new consumerism was a marvel of modern life, providing people a level of comfort, leisure, and self-expression unimaginable to previous generations. For its critics, however, the consumer culture threatened long-established virtues such as hard work, plain living, and prudent money management.

Word help: recession = a time when business slows down · emergence = the start of something · mass production = making huge numbers of the same product · leisure = free time · virtues = good habits · prudent = careful

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 22, “A “New Era” of Consumption” (A Growing Consumer Culture) (p. 948).

Reading BAds, Credit, Movies, and Radio

What was new in the 1920s was not just the goods being sold, but how businesses sold them. Marketing and advertising came of age during the decade. “Layaway” plans and installment buying encouraged consumers to “buy now, pay later.” As a result, consumer debt almost tripled during the decade.

Mass advertising, mass production, and the mass media combined to create a mass culture. Increasingly, Americans in all regions of the country read the same magazines, listened to the same radio programs, watched the same movies, and drove the same kinds of cars. They saw the same ads and shopped at the same national retail stores.

Movie attendance during the 1920s averaged 80 million people a week; attendance surged even more after 1927, when “talking” movies appeared. . . . Between 1922 and 1930, the number of families owning a radio skyrocketed from 60,000 to nearly 14 million.

Word help: installment buying = paying a little each month · consumer debt = money people owe for things they bought · mass media = movies, radio, and magazines that reach millions · surged = went up fast

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 22, “A “New Era” of Consumption” (A Growing Consumer Culture; The Rise of Mass Culture; A Love Affair with Movies; The Radio Craze).

Reading CThe Car Culture

The most significant economic and social development of the early twentieth century was the widespread ownership of automobiles.

Ford’s Model T, affordable and durable, appeared in 1908 at a price of $850 (about $28,000 in today’s dollars). By 1924, his increasingly efficient production techniques enabled him to sell the same car for $290. . . . In 1916, the total number of cars in the United States passed 1 million; by 1920, more than 8 million were registered; and in 1929 there were more than 23 million.

The automobile changed social behavior. A car not only provided greater mobility and speed; it offered freedom. In the words of one male driver, young people viewed the car as “an incredible engine of escape” from parental oversight and control.

Word help: durable = lasts a long time · efficient = getting more done with less · mobility = ability to move around · oversight = watching over

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 22, “A “New Era” of Consumption” (The Car Culture).

Picture 1Ford’s Highland Park Plant, 1913

This photo shows cars being built at a Ford Motor Company factory in 1913. Chain conveyors moved each car frame (chassis) down the assembly line. (It is a primary source.)

What to look for: assembly line = a line where each worker does one job as the product moves past · chassis = the frame and wheels of a car · conveyor = a moving belt or chain that carries parts

Norton, Ch. 22, “A “New Era” of Consumption,” caption: “Highland Park Plant, 1913. The Ford Motor Company led the way in efficiency and cost-cutting production methods.” Primary source.

Part 2 of 7

The Jazz Age and the “New Woman”

CORE OBJECTIVE

Core Objective 2: Describe other major new social and cultural trends and movements that became prominent during the 1920s and explain how they challenged traditional standards and customs.

IN MY WORDS: Name one new trend of the 1920s and one old custom it challenged.

Reading DThe Jazz Age

During the 1920s, many young people eagerly participated in a social and cultural rebellion—trying new fads and fashions, new music, new attitudes, and new ways of having fun.

He fastened upon the phrase Jazz Age as the evocative label for the rebellious, spontaneous, and sensual decade of the 1920s, the “greatest, gaudiest spree in history.”

The culture of jazz quickly spread from its origins in New Orleans, Kansas City, Memphis, and St. Louis to the African American neighborhoods of Harlem in New York City and Chicago’s South Side. Large dance halls met the swelling demand for jazz music and the dance craze that accompanied it, including new dances such as the Charleston and the Black Bottom whose sexually provocative movements shocked traditionalists.

Word help: He = F. Scott Fitzgerald, a famous writer of the 1920s · rebellion = fighting against rules · evocative = bringing a strong picture to mind · spontaneous = done on the spur of the moment · gaudiest = flashiest · traditionalists = people who want to keep the old ways

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 22, “The “Jazz Age”” (F. Scott Fitzgerald: The Voice of a Generation; The Birth of Jazz).

Reading EFlappers and Not-So-“New” Women

In 1919, skirts were typically six inches above the ground; by 1927, they were at the knee. The shortest ones were worn by the so-called flappers, young women who—in defiance of prevailing standards—“bobbed” their hair (cut it short, requiring the invention of the “bobby pin”) and wore minimal underclothing, gauzy fabrics, sheer stockings, and plenty of makeup, especially brightly colored rouge and lipstick and smoky mascara. They also joined young men in driving automobiles, smoking cigarettes, (illegally) drinking and gambling, and shaking and shimmying to the sensual energies of jazz music.

Most women in the 1920s were not rebels like Margaret Sanger or flappers like Zelda Fitzgerald, however. . . . Fewer college-educated women pursued careers outside the home. As before, most women who worked outside the home labored in unskilled, low-paying jobs. Only 4 percent of working women were salaried professionals.

Word help: Margaret Sanger = a nurse who fought for birth control · Zelda Fitzgerald = a famous flapper, the writer’s wife · defiance = openly refusing to obey · prevailing standards = the usual rules · salaried professionals = workers in high-paying careers

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 22, “The “Jazz Age”” (Women in the 1920s; Not-So-“New” Women).

Source 1Amelia Earhart on Women and Flying (Primary Source)

Amelia Earhart was the first woman to fly across the Atlantic Ocean. In 1928 she wrote about women in aviation (flying). Chrysler was a brand of car.

“Generally speaking, women control the purchasing power of the modern economic world. It is a brave man who buys another make when his wife wants a Chrysler! . . . A similar influence inevitably will be exerted in connection with air transport—if women will fly. As they became an important factor in passenger revenue their requirements will be increasingly studied and met. . . . Today there are ample facilities for flying instruction throughout the United States. It is, however, considerably more difficult for a woman to procure it than it is for a man.”

Word help: purchasing power = the money to buy things · make = brand · inevitably = for sure · exerted = used · passenger revenue = money from people buying plane tickets · ample = plenty · procure = get

Amelia Earhart, “Women in Aviation,” in 20 hrs. 40 min.: Our Flight in the Friendship, 1928. In Norton, Ch. 22, “The “Jazz Age”,” Comparing Perspectives: “Culture and Celebrity in the Jazz Age.”

Source 1. According to Earhart, who controls most buying? What is still harder for a woman than for a man?

Point of view. Earhart was a famous woman pilot. Why might she want readers to believe that women matter to the new economy?

Part 3 of 7

Harlem and the Modernist Revolt

CORE OBJECTIVES

Core Objective 2: Describe other major new social and cultural trends and movements that became prominent during the 1920s and explain how they challenged traditional standards and customs.

Core Objective 3: Explain what “modernism” means in intellectual and artistic terms and how the modernist movement influenced American culture in the early twentieth century.

IN MY WORDS: What was the Harlem Renaissance? What did modernist artists want to do?

Reading FThe Harlem Renaissance

As their Great Migration from the segregated South continued into the 1920s, African Americans found freedoms in northern settings; they also gained leverage as voters by settling in high-population states with many electoral votes. Along with these new opportunities came a bristling spirit of creativity and protest known as the Harlem Renaissance, the nation’s first Black literary and artistic movement.

By 1930, the Harlem-based writers had produced dozens of novels and volumes of poetry; several Broadway plays; and a flood of short stories, essays, and films. A people capable of producing such great art and literature, James Weldon Johnson declared, should never again be “looked upon as inferior.” The art produced during the Harlem Renaissance was a powerful assertion of the intelligence, creativity, and dignity of Black Americans.

Word help: leverage = power to get what you want · electoral votes = votes that choose the president · Renaissance = rebirth, a time of new art · assertion = strong statement · dignity = self-respect

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 22, “The “Jazz Age”” (The Harlem Renaissance).

Reading GRestrictive Covenants and the Sweet Case

At that time, racially restrictive covenants—legal agreements whereby neighborhood residents pledged not to sell their homes to poor or non-White buyers—remained common. In September 1925, when the Sweet family moved in, they were greeted by a mob of local White residents.

The NAACP hired the celebrated attorney Clarence Darrow to represent the Sweets. He convinced the jury that the long-established right to use force to defend one’s home applied equally to all people, regardless of their skin color. It was a landmark victory for the NAACP, although housing discrimination against non-Whites would persist for decades to come.

Word help: the Sweets = the family of Ossian Sweet, a Black doctor in Detroit · covenants = written promises in a deal · pledged = promised · NAACP = a group that fought for Black civil rights · landmark = very important · persist = keep going

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 22, “The “Jazz Age”” (The NAACP and Housing Discrimination).

Reading HWhat Was Modernism?

Modernism was an intellectual, literary, and artistic movement that appeared first in the capitals of Europe—London, Paris, Berlin, and Vienna—in the 1890s. By the second decade of the twentieth century, cultural modernism had spread to the United States, especially New York City and Chicago.

To be a “modern” writer or painter or dancer was to break free of tradition, violate artistic rules and moral restrictions, and behave in deliberately shocking ways. “Art,” said a modernist painter, “is meant to disturb.” . . . Experimental poet Ezra Pound provided the slogan for modernism when he exclaimed, “Make It New!”

Word help: intellectual = about ideas · literary = about books and writing · tradition = the old ways · violate = break · disturb = upset

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 22, “The Modernist Revolt”.

Reading IEinstein and “Relativity”

Einstein revolutionized notions of time, space, and light. Although only a few scholars understood the details of his theories, many began to embrace the idea that there were no absolute standards or fixed points of reference in the world. During the 1920s, the idea of “relativity” gradually emerged in popular discussions of decidedly nonscientific topics such as sexuality, the arts, and politics; there was less faith in absolutes, not only of time and space but also of truth, morality, and traditional religion.

Word help: revolutionized = completely changed · absolutes = things that are always true · morality = ideas of right and wrong

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 22, “The Modernist Revolt” (Science and Modernism: Einstein and Relativity).

Part 4 of 7

Nativism and Immigration Limits

CORE OBJECTIVE

Core Objective 4: Identify notable examples of reactionary conservatism during the decade and analyze their impact on government policies.

IN MY WORDS: What is nativism? How did it change immigration laws in the 1920s?

Reading JFear of Change and Nativism

For most Americans, the frivolity and excess of the Jazz Age were just something they read about in magazines. They were not disillusioned, self-destructive, or defiantly modernist. Most people still led traditional lives based on established values, old certainties, and the comfort of past routines. For many of them, the decade’s social turmoil and cultural rebelliousness were both shocking and scary.

This defense of traditionalism in the 1920s was rooted in a sense of nativism—that is, prejudice against any non-native-born people. In this case, the targets of nativist prejudice were Catholic and Jewish immigrants from southern and eastern Europe.

Word help: frivolity = silly fun · disillusioned = no longer believing in old hopes · turmoil = confusion and trouble · prejudice = unfair dislike of a group

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 22, “The Reactionary Twenties”.

Reading KThe Immigration Act of 1924

The Immigration Act of 1924 (the National Origins Act) reduced the number (“quota”) of visas from 3 percent to 2 percent of the total number of people of each nationality in the United States as of the 1890 census. The goal was to lock in place the racial and ethnic balance of the country—maintaining a large White Protestant majority—that had existed almost thirty years earlier, before the massive wave of southern- and eastern-European immigration at the turn of the twentieth century.

The law, in essence, created a hierarchy for determining who should be admitted to the country. Immigrants from northern and western Europe were at the top. Much further down were immigrants from southern and eastern Europe. Asians were at the bottom. Under the quota system, more than 50,000 Germans could enter the nation annually, while fewer than 4,000 Italians were allowed.

President Calvin Coolidge readily signed the immigration restriction bill, insisting that “America must be kept American.”

Word help: quota = a set number allowed · census = an official count of the people · hierarchy = a ranking from top to bottom · annually = each year

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 22, “The Reactionary Twenties” (Reactionary Politics and Immigration Restriction).

Picture 2Foreign-Born Population in the United States in 1920

This chart from the 1920s shows how many people living in the United States in 1920 were born in each country. Norton says these numbers “formed the basis of the quota system” in the Immigration Act of 1924. (It is a primary source.)

What to look for: foreign-born = born in another country · the size of each figure = how many people came from that country · Roumania = Romania

Norton, Ch. 22, “The Reactionary Twenties,” caption: “Immigration Act of 1924. This immigration chart illustrates the nationalities of the foreign-born population in the United States in 1920.” Primary source.

Picture 2. (1) Which two countries had the most foreign-born people in the United States in 1920? (2) Italy was second on this chart. Use Reading K: how many Italians could enter each year under the new quota?

Reading LSacco and Vanzetti and the Second Klan

The most celebrated criminal case of the 1920s reinforced the connection between European immigrants and political radicalism. On May 5, 1920, two Italian immigrants who described themselves as revolutionary anarchists eager to topple the American government were arrested outside Boston, Massachusetts.

In July 1921, Sacco and Vanzetti were convicted and sentenced to death. Their legal appeals lasted six years before they were electrocuted on August 23, 1927, still claiming innocence. To millions around the world, Sacco and Vanzetti were victims of capitalist injustice. People still debate their guilt.

The most violent of the reactionary movements during the 1920s was a revived Ku Klux Klan. . . . Now, no longer simply a southern group intent on terrorizing African Americans, the new Klan was a nationwide organization devoted to “100 percent Americanism”; only “natives”—White Protestants born in the United States—could be members.

Word help: radicalism = wanting big, sudden change · anarchists = people who want no government · topple = knock down · convicted = found guilty · revived = brought back

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 22, “The Reactionary Twenties” (Sacco and Vanzetti; The Second Klan).

Think about it. The Sacco and Vanzetti case happened at a time of fear of immigrants. Why do you think millions of people around the world believed the two men were treated unfairly?

Part 5 of 7

Fundamentalism, Scopes, and Prohibition

CORE OBJECTIVE

Core Objective 4: Identify notable examples of reactionary conservatism during the decade and analyze their impact on government policies.

IN MY WORDS: Name one way reactionary conservatives tried to use the law to protect traditional ways.

Reading MFundamentalism and the Scopes Trial

The pamphlets sparked a new term and a movement, fundamentalism, that insisted on the literal truth of the Bible, embraced a strict return to Christian orthodoxy, and was deeply skeptical of “liberal” beliefs of all sorts. While most American Christians fell somewhere between the poles of modernism and fundamentalism, the debate between the two became a front line in the cultural wars of the 1920s.

In 1925, the Tennessee state legislature had outlawed the teaching of evolution in public schools and colleges. Enterprising civic leaders in the tiny mining town of Dayton, Tennessee, eager for publicity, persuaded John T. Scopes, a twenty-four-year-old high-school science teacher, to become a test case against the new law.

As the trial ended, the judge ruled that the only issue before the jury was whether John T. Scopes had taught evolution, and no one had denied that he had done so.

But the Tennessee Supreme Court, while upholding the anti-evolution law, waived Scopes’s $100 fine on a technicality. Both sides claimed victory. . . . Meanwhile, the Scopes Trial only sharpened the national debate between fundamentalism and evolution that continues today.

Word help: The pamphlets = booklets called The Fundamentals, written by conservative Protestants · literal = word for word, exactly as written · orthodoxy = the traditional beliefs · skeptical = doubtful · evolution = the theory that living things change over time · test case = a case meant to challenge a law · waived = canceled

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 22, “The Reactionary Twenties” (Fundamentalism; The Scopes Trial).

Reading NProhibition

On December 18, 1917, Congress sent to the states the Eighteenth Amendment. Ratified on January 16, 1919, it banned “the manufacture, sale, and transportation of intoxicating liquors,” effective one year later.

Prohibition was thus the law during the 1920s—but it was not widely followed. As the most ambitious social reform ever attempted in the United States, it proved to be a colossal and costly failure. It was too sweeping for the government to enforce and too frustrating for most Americans to respect, and it had many unforeseen consequences.

The loss of liquor taxes, for example, cost the federal government almost 30 percent of its annual revenue. The closing of breweries, distilleries, and saloons eliminated thousands of jobs. Even more consequential were the huge number of Americans who broke the law and the enormous boost that Prohibition gave to police corruption and to organized crime.

Word help: ratified = officially approved · intoxicating liquors = alcoholic drinks · colossal = huge · unforeseen consequences = results no one expected · revenue = money the government takes in

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 22, “The Reactionary Twenties” (Prohibition).

Part 6 of 7

Republicans in Charge

CORE OBJECTIVE

Core Objective 5: Trace the Republican Party’s dominance of the federal government during the 1920s and analyze the extent to which its policies were a rejection of progressivism.

IN MY WORDS: Did the Republican presidents of the 1920s keep progressive reforms or roll them back? Give one example.

Reading OHarding and “Normalcy”

After the Great War, Progressivism lost its momentum but did not disappear entirely. The progressive crusade for honest, efficient government and tighter regulation of business remained strong, especially at the state and local levels, where efforts to improve public education, public health, and social-welfare programs gained momentum. At the national level, however, conservative Republicans returned to power.

Harding set out to reverse the progressive activism of Woodrow Wilson and Theodore Roosevelt and reassert the primacy of Congress over the presidency. He and his lieutenants dismantled or neutralized many progressive regulatory laws and agencies.

During the 1920s, the Taft-led Court struck down a federal child-labor law and a minimum-wage law for women, issued numerous injunctions against striking labor unions, and passed rulings limiting the powers of federal agencies that regulated large corporations.

Word help: momentum = forward energy · normalcy = a return to normal times · dismantled = took apart · regulatory = making rules for businesses · injunctions = court orders to stop something

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 22, “Republican Resurgence” (Warren Harding and “Normalcy”; Harding’s Personality and Associates) (p. 983).

Reading PTaxes, Unions, Race, and Scandal

To generate economic growth, Secretary of the Treasury Andrew Mellon, the third richest man in the world behind John D. Rockefeller and Henry Ford, called for reducing federal spending, lowering tax rates, and raising tariffs on imported goods. . . . Government expenditures fell, as did the national debt, and the economy soared. Unemployment plummeted to 2.4 percent in 1923.

Such anti-union efforts succeeded in reducing union membership from about 5 million in 1920 to 3.5 million in 1929.

The most serious controversy was the Teapot Dome Scandal. The Teapot Dome was a government-owned oil field in Wyoming managed by the Department of the Interior. Secretary of the Interior Albert B. Fall, deeply in debt and eight years overdue in paying his taxes, began secretly selling the oil to close friends who were executives of petroleum companies. In doing so, Fall took huge bribes from two oil tycoons.

Word help: anti-union efforts = actions by business owners to stop workers from joining unions · tariffs = taxes on goods from other countries · expenditures = money spent · tycoons = very rich business owners · bribes = money paid to get someone to do something wrong

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 22, “Republican Resurgence” (Andrew Mellon and the Economy; Setbacks for Unions; The Harding Scandals).

Reading QCoolidge: “The Business of America”

Even more than Harding, Coolidge sought to reduce the size and scope of the federal government and to promote business interests. “The chief business of the American people is business,” he preached. “The man who builds a factory builds a temple. The man who works there worships there.”

Thus, the highly trumpeted “new economy” of the 1920s was not benefiting enough working-class Americans to be sustainable. The gap between income levels and purchasing power would be a significant factor leading to the Great Depression, as the Republican formula of high tariffs, low wages, low taxes, little regulation, and anti-unionism would eventually implode.

Word help: sustainable = able to last · purchasing power = the money to buy things · implode = collapse

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 22, “Republican Resurgence” (A Do-Nothing President—By Design; Setbacks for Unions).
